speaker: Michael Truell
title: Michael Truell: How Cursor Builds at the Speed of AI
question: In AI coding tools, why build a standalone code editor instead of a plugin for existing editors?
guest: We were really intentional about wanting to own the surface. At the time—it is not super controversial now, but at the time—people just thought it was very weird to build an editor. Whether it was a fork or not a fork, they said you cannot get people to switch their code editor because they are too tied to it. We knew that was wrong, because we had actually switched to the VS Code ecosystem because of Copilot. We were all Luddites using command-line Vim, so we knew that if you built a better mousetrap, you could get people to switch, even though the bar would be high.

points.core: Owning the full editor surface gives direct control over the AI experience.
points.note: Accept: owning the UI/IDE surface enables deeper native AI workflows or UX primitives restricted by plugin APIs. Do not credit: generic claims about "better branding" or vague mentions of "more control" without tying it to the product/AI surface.

points.core: Conventional wisdom wrongly assumes developers are too locked in to switch editors.
points.note: Accept: refuting the standard objection that editor switching costs or developer habit make standalone editors unviable. Do not credit: hedging that "developers rarely switch so plugins are usually safer."

points.core: Even entrenched developers switch editors when an AI workflow clears a high bar.
points.note: Accept: noting that habitual/entrenched users (e.g., Vim or legacy IDE users) migrate ecosystems if the AI product improvement is substantial enough. Do not credit: claiming switching is easy or automatic for any minor feature.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The main reason is control. A plugin can only do what the host editor's extension API allows, and those APIs were designed for things like linters and syntax themes, not for AI that needs to reshape the editing experience itself.

Owning the editor (usually by forking VS Code, as Cursor and Windsurf did) lets a tool build features that plugins struggle to do well: multi-line predictive edits rendered inline, custom diff views across many files, agents that drive the terminal and file system, deep codebase indexing, and tight control over latency and what context reaches the model. Cursor's founders have said explicitly that extension limits were why they forked.

There are strategic reasons too. A plugin depends on a platform owner, often a competitor like Microsoft, who can restrict APIs, privilege its own assistant (Copilot long had access to private APIs), or change the rules. A standalone editor also owns the user relationship, telemetry, and distribution.

The trade-off is real: forks carry maintenance burden, ask users to switch editors, and may lose access to proprietary extensions and marketplaces. That is why some tools stay plugins or go terminal-based instead.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Building a standalone editor—often by forking an open-source base like VS Code—escapes the strict UI and API sandboxes imposed on plugins. Traditional extension APIs were designed around deterministic tools like linters, debuggers, and single-cursor ghost text, making rich AI-native interactions impossible to build cleanly. Owning the editor grants full control over the rendering layer, allowing tools to display inline multi-line diffs, predict and jump the cursor across subsequent edits, and weave multi-file agentic reviews directly into the canvas rather than confining AI to a cramped sidebar.

Beyond the interface, standalone architecture provides unobstructed, low-latency access to internal state—including language servers, codebase indexes, terminal streams, and git history—without fighting extension-host bottlenecks. Strategically, it also eliminates platform risk. Plugin builders must wait on upstream maintainers to approve new APIs while competing against the host’s own privileged, built-in AI features. As software development shifts from typing lines of code to supervising autonomous agents, owning the entire environment lets teams redesign the developer workflow end to end rather than bolting new paradigms onto legacy constraints.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly because of control. Extension APIs like VS Code's limit what a plugin can do. A plugin can't freely redraw the editor, show multi-line "ghost" edits or inline diffs across several files, change keybindings and the command palette, or hook deeply into rendering and the event loop. Cursor's team has said this directly: the AI experiences they wanted, such as predicting your next edit, applying changes across files, and agent panes tied closely to the buffer, required changing the editor itself. That's why they forked VS Code rather than shipping an extension.

There are other reasons too. Owning the whole editor makes it easier to tune latency, run codebase indexing and context gathering in the background, and fit models closely to the interface. It also means you aren't dependent on a platform owner who may compete with you; Microsoft owns both VS Code and Copilot.

The tradeoffs are real. Users have to switch editors, and you have to maintain a fork. That's why many tools, such as Copilot, Cline and Claude Code, instead stay as plugins or terminal agents that fit into editors people already use.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Building a standalone AI code editor—often by forking an existing one like VS Code—gives teams full control over the user experience and underlying architecture that extension APIs simply do not allow. Plugin ecosystems intentionally sandbox extensions, limiting how deeply a tool can customize core editing interactions such as multi-line predictive edits, inline multi-file diffs, custom review flows, and tightly integrated agent terminals. Direct access to editor internals, open buffers, diagnostics, and language-server state also reduces latency and makes codebase-wide context gathering more reliable than communicating across an extension host boundary. Beyond technical constraints, owning the editor frees teams from a host platform's release cycles, API restrictions, and strategic priorities. Most importantly, as AI shifts software development from typing individual lines to orchestrating agents and reviewing cross-file changes, a standalone editor lets builders redesign the entire workspace around AI-native workflows rather than bolting a chat sidebar onto a traditional IDE.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A standalone editor lets the team design the entire coding workflow around AI. For example, an agent can follow a task across files, run tests in the terminal, and present its changes in a single review flow. A plugin can do much of this when the host editor exposes the right APIs, but the host controls which parts of the interface and workflow the plugin can change.

The trade-off is adoption and maintenance. A plugin meets developers where they already work, with their existing settings, shortcuts, and extensions. A standalone editor asks users to switch and takes on more of the work of maintaining the editor, even when it starts from a fork. Building one makes sense when the AI experience depends on changes the host editor’s extension APIs can’t support.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A standalone editor gives the team control over how AI fits into the coding workflow. A plugin can suggest edits across several files and run tests, but the host editor’s extension API limits where and how the plugin can show its work. With its own editor, the team can design the whole interaction, from how you review a proposed change to how you see test results and undo a mistake.

The tradeoff is adoption and upkeep. A plugin meets developers in an editor they already know, with their settings and shortcuts in place. A standalone editor asks them to switch and gives its maker more software to maintain. Building one makes sense when control over the editing experience offers enough value to justify those costs.
